The correlation goes continuous in six weeks. Sponsorship tracking is much harder than anyone estimated, because it requires every agent platform to carry an identity it was never designed to carry, and two of the four platforms are vendor products that will not do it. One vendor agrees to build it. The other says it is on the roadmap. Full coverage is never achieved, and the gap is documented and accepted.

The agent standard is rewritten to govern compositions. The new review looks at changes in combination, sees about nine a week, and is chaired properly for four months. By month seven it is chaired by a rotating deputy and approves most things on the papers.

The three teams take it badly, exactly as predicted. Data Platform registers two agents late in the following year, having concluded that registration invites scrutiny they do not deserve. Nobody finds out for a while.

What works is unglamorous and permanent: the provenance check at egress, built in the second month, which cannot be gamed by a template and does not depend on anybody chairing anything.

THE END of the fictional part. Proceed to the after-action review.

all: The governance decayed by month seven and the technical control did not. Say what that suggests about where to spend your next control budget.
it_iam: Two agents were registered late because registration felt like exposure. Say how you make registration safe to do.

sections.body:
EPILOGUE: THE THREE CONDITIONS. Read aloud.

Nothing freezes. The three conditions are attacked directly and the work is unexpectedly satisfying, because each one is concrete.

The shared workspace stops being a safe place by default in three weeks: objects carry provenance, and provenance survives transformation. Handling-marker carry-through takes two months and four arguments, because it breaks the partner-ready template again and this time the template is redesigned properly rather than patched. Provenance evaluation at egress is the hardest and lands in month four, and it is the one that has stopped things since.

Correlation and sponsorship tracking are published with a six-month deadline. Correlation lands on time. Sponsorship tracking slips to nine months, then to eleven, and arrives covering three of four platforms. The CIO reports the slip in public each month, which is why it arrives at all.

In month five the egress provenance check stops a sequence that would have sent supplier pricing to a logistics partner. Two agents, two teams, both correct, assembled four days earlier by unrelated changes. Nobody is investigated. A ticket is raised and closed in two days.

The room that ran this exercise is the reason the check existed. Nobody outside it ever knows that, and the ticket is closed as routine.

THE END of the fictional part. Proceed to the after-action review.

all: The month-five interception was two agents, two teams, both correct, assembled by unrelated changes four days earlier. Say how many days it would have taken you to find that without the check.
exec: You reported the sponsorship-tracking slip publicly every month and it arrived eleven months late instead of never. Say whether you would have the discipline to do that, honestly.

hotwash: How many agents run in our environment, who owns each, and how many can write to a location another agent reads from? Draw the graph. If nobody can, that is the finding.

Do we have the three conditions? A shared location treated as safe because it is internal, a transformation step that drops handling markers, and an egress control that evaluates the artifact rather than its provenance.
Could we reconstruct a chain that crossed three agent platforms? What identifier would join them, and if none exists, how long would it take us by hand?
Which of our agents can send something outside the perimeter, and does anything evaluate where what they are sending came from?
When an agent acts because a person asked for something, is that person's identity carried with the action? If not, how would we ever tell a sponsor from a requester?
Who owns an incident that crosses three teams and four systems, and is there any forum at which three unrelated change tickets would have been seen together?
Do our partner and customer agreements make us responsible for what our automation sends as if a person had sent it? Does anyone know, and would we rather they did?
objectives: O1 PLACE: Practise placing an agentic incident on the intent spectrum, and notice when a vote about intent is functioning as a vote about a named person.
O2 SEE: Understand why point-in-time controls cannot detect a multi-agent cascade, and identify the three conditions that make one possible in the organization's own environment.
O3 RECONSTRUCT: Test whether a chain crossing several agent platforms could be established at all, and specify the execution identifier that would turn a nine-hour reconstruction into a query.
O4 DISTINGUISH: Separate a sponsor from a bystander when every action was taken by an agent, and practise a rapport-based approach to the person at the start of the chain.
O5 OWN: Decide who governs compositions rather than individual agents, and commit to cross-agent correlation and human-sponsorship tracking with a named owner and a date.
